speaker: Doctor
text: Hello, I am Dr. Agent. Please describe the neck swelling you are experiencing, including how long it has been present and if it is painful or changing in size.

speaker: Patient
text: 50-year-old male. The patient reports a progressively increasing swelling on the nape of his neck for 2 months. He denies having a fever, pain, or any discharge from the swelling. He mentions a history of colon cancer for which he underwent colectomy at the age of 43. He also has a history of type 2 diabetes mellitus, hypertension, and osteoarthritis of the left knee. He takes insulin glargine, metformin, enalapril, and naproxen.

speaker: Doctor
text: Thank you for the details. Given your history of colon cancer and current neck swelling, I need to know if you have noticed any other lumps in your neck or armpits, or if you have experienced any unexplained weight loss or fatigue over the last two months. REQUEST TEST: Complete Blood Count (CBC) and Comprehensive Metabolic Panel (CMP).

speaker: Measurement
text: RESULTS: Complete Blood Count (CBC): Normal; Comprehensive Metabolic Panel (CMP): Glucose - Elevated, Creatinine - Normal, Liver Enzymes - Normal.

speaker: Doctor
text: The blood work confirms your diabetes but shows no sign of infection in your blood. Given your history of colon cancer, this persistent, painless lump on the nape of your neck is highly suspicious for a metastatic deposit. REQUEST TEST: Neck_Ultrasound to evaluate the characteristics of the swelling.

speaker: Measurement
text: RESULTS: Ultrasound of the Neck: Well-circumscribed lesion in the subcutaneous tissue suggestive of a cystic nature.

speaker: Doctor
text: The ultrasound suggests a cystic lesion rather than a solid metastatic deposit, which is unexpected given your history. Have you noticed any changes in your voice, difficulty swallowing, or hoarseness recently? REQUEST IMAGES: Neck_Ultrasound for further review.

speaker: Doctor
text:
DIAGNOSIS READY: Branchial Cleft Cyst (Second Branchial Cleft Cyst).

While your history of colon cancer raises concern for metastasis, the ultrasound showing a well-circumscribed cystic lesion in the subcutaneous tissue of the nape of the neck is characteristic of a congenital branchial cleft cyst, which can become symptomatic later in life. I am confident this is benign, but please proceed with surgical excision for definitive diagnosis and to prevent future infection.
